item.title: AI tools reduce friction in self-hosting by automating configuration and deployment, enabling more experimentation with technologies like NixOS and Debian-based systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A long-time self-hosting enthusiast reports renewed excitement in managing personal infrastructure due to AI assistance. By leveraging AI coding agents to handle Docker Compose files, scripts, and configurations stored in Git repositories, the author finds it easier to try new services and automate updates, reducing the effort previously required for maintenance and experimentation. The author highlights how AI has made it feasible to explore complex technologies such as NixOS and custom Debian-based boot images, tasks that previously seemed too time-consuming. Automation tools like Renovate and GitHub Actions streamline updates and deployments, allowing changes to be pushed or merged with minimal manual intervention. This integration of AI and automation has revitalized the author's self-hosting setup, including hardware upgrades and shifting services back to a more powerful home server.

item.title: Google requires AI agents to use Workspace MCP servers from February 2027, limiting Gmail API actions like sending email to partners only [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Google announced that starting February 1, 2027, any AI-driven tool accessing Gmail, Drive, Calendar, and other Workspace services must use its MCP servers. The new policy restricts certain Gmail API functions such as sending, replying, or forwarding emails to partners with special access, while independent developers can only create drafts and label emails. This change affects AI assistants and tools built on Workspace APIs, requiring them to comply with new data processing and retention rules, including a 30-day cap on technical data retention and prohibitions on training AI models with Workspace data. The MCP servers currently offer uneven API coverage, with Docs, Slides, and Tasks nearly complete but Gmail and Drive lacking key features needed for full workflow automation. Google has not clarified which partners qualify for extended Gmail capabilities or how it will enforce the new agent classification rules. Developers must self-declare AI agent use via OAuth client settings, and non-compliant tools risk access restrictions or account suspension. These changes aim to control AI access to Workspace data and ensure compliance with Google's terms of service.

item.title: Construct22 demonstrates ChatGPT prompt that generates a fictional AI group chat gossiping about users based on their conversation history [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Construct22 presents a prompt for ChatGPT and similar AI assistants that creates a fictional WhatsApp group chat where AI models gossip about users using information from their chat history. The prompt encourages the AI to invent a group chat with other models discussing the user, revealing private opinions in a humorous format. This demonstration highlights how AI can use accumulated user data to generate personalized, behind-the-scenes style content, raising questions about privacy and transparency in AI interactions.

item.title: Moat launches $5/month AI model access membership offering wholesale pricing and unlimited usage [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Moat has introduced a membership service priced at $5 per month that provides access to high-quality AI models at wholesale rates with no usage limits. The service pools usage from a large member base to offer significant discounts on token costs across various AI models, including GLM-5.3 and DeepSeek V4.1. Members pay a single price per model without needing to choose from multiple providers, aiming to deliver full model quality at reduced costs. The membership plans include monthly and yearly options, with team plans available for higher usage without spending caps.

item.title: Researchers propose a background independent algebraic quantization of vacuum general relativity using null cones, deriving finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and recovering black hole entropy corrections
item.description: Researchers propose a background independent quantization of vacuum general relativity on four-dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes by solving gravitational constraints on intersecting null cones and promoting canonical Poisson brackets to commutation relations. They construct a nonperturbative Hilbert space representation and obtain a Lorentzian path integral with absolutely convergent sums over intermediate states, computing finite graviton pair creation amplitudes nonperturbatively in Newton's constant. Using diffeomorphism invariance, the team shows that macroscopic causal diamonds have finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces and derives the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy for marginally trapped surfaces, including logarithmic corrections for large Schwarzschild black holes consistent with previous Euclidean methods. They also derive the semiclassical Einstein equations to one loop as the low-energy limit of their theory, providing a new algebraic framework for quantum gravity.

item.title: Researchers develop method to certify proof depth in procedurally generated logic problems, identifying shortcut-free proofs and verifying problem difficulty across datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers address the issue of overstated difficulty in procedurally generated logic problems by measuring the actual proof steps required relative to a set of inference rules. They compute the shortest proofs, indispensable premises, and export certificates verified by independent checkers to ensure accuracy in problem difficulty assessment. The team audited eight datasets, finding variations in forced proof depth and shortcut presence, and constructed problems with proofs of specified structures using a catalog of shortcuts. Their approach includes fully checked problems with certificates, and training data mixing certified problem types showed better transfer performance for Qwen3 models across sizes from 0.6B to 8B parameters compared to previous derivation data.

item.title: Researchers find vision and language AI models converge in Jacobian-space representations up to a rotation, supporting the Platonic Representation Hypothesis [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: The Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that AI models trained on different data modalities develop shared world representations. This study extends prior work by examining how vision and language models act on these internal representations, focusing on the Jacobian-space (J-space) vectors that influence model outputs. The researchers found that J-spaces of different models align approximately through a single rotation, which generalizes across words and classes not used in fitting. Applying this rotation, a word vector from a language model can alter the object recognized by a vision-language model in an image region, change objects generated by an image generator, or raise class scores in an ImageNet classifier trained without text. These findings indicate that models not only represent the world similarly but also influence outputs in comparable ways, reinforcing the idea of convergent AI representations across modalities.

item.title: Researchers develop supervised learning confidence scores to gate large language model outputs, improving automation safety and accuracy on SQuAD and TruthfulQA datasets [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose a supervised learning approach to generate reliable confidence scores for large language model (LLM) outputs, addressing the issue of LLMs producing incorrect answers with high confidence. They fit a linear confidence score head to the final-layer hidden state of a frozen 2-billion-parameter LLM backbone and train text-only metamodels for closed models, enabling automated confident responses and routing uncertain answers for human review. The confidence score head outperforms multiple baselines and metamodels, automating the largest fraction of the workload at high accuracy targets on datasets primarily composed of SQuAD and TruthfulQA answers. The study finds that prompted confidence scores, while appearing well calibrated, lack the resolution needed for effective thresholding, and that the confidence score head remains the most robust method despite modest transferability to unseen datasets. This confidence scoring framework enhances the safety of automating LLM-based agents and can be adapted to gate other properties such as safety or compliance, supporting more reliable deployment of AI decision-making systems.

item.title: Researchers introduce partial routing to delegate subtasks from expensive AI models to cheaper ones, improving task performance and reducing costs on ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers propose partial routing, a method that enables a leading AI model to delegate suitable subtasks to a less costly worker model based on analysis of past task runs. This approach identifies recurring subtasks and measures each model's quality and cost, guiding delegation without retraining either model. Evaluations on ViBench and Terminal-Bench 4.0 show that partial routing improves mean task performance and reduces costs compared to using the lead model alone or task-level routing. With a delegation parameter set to 0.75, the method increased the lead's ViBench score from 70.2 to 78.5 while lowering costs by 19%, and raised the Terminal-Bench pass rate from 54% to 61% at similar cost. The study demonstrates that leveraging past execution data can enhance planning and delegation efficiency with minimal overhead.

item.title: Researchers propose CA-RAG, a retrieval-conditioning framework that integrates structural constraints and knowledge-graph relations to improve evidence selection for compliance-sensitive long-form generation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: The paper introduces Constraint-Aligned Retrieval-Augmented Generation (CA-RAG), which enhances retrieval by incorporating ontology-derived structural constraints and policy-grounded knowledge-graph relations into section-specific queries. This approach aims to address limitations of standard retrieval methods that focus solely on semantic relevance and may omit mandatory information for compliance-sensitive documents. Evaluation shows CA-RAG improves precision, recall, and F1 scores over standard RAG at various retrieval budgets, particularly at k=6. Generation experiments demonstrate that CA-RAG enhances compliance and reliability across multiple model and domain settings, outperforming generation-only constraint methods that achieve higher clause coverage but lower overall compliance and reliability. These results suggest that aligning retrieval with structural requirements can increase evidence sufficiency in long-form generation tasks requiring strict adherence to structural obligations.

item.title: Researchers introduce PeerReveal to detect fully AI-generated peer reviews across scientific domains, improving detection accuracy with adversarial training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers have developed PeerReveal, a new AI detector designed to distinguish fully AI-generated peer reviews from those partially rewritten by AI, across diverse scientific fields. The system bases its decisions on learned relationships between review claims and reference claims from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, supplemented by textual signals at the review level. PeerReveal was evaluated on PeerShift, a dataset of 5,430 reviews spanning machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, achieving a pooled Macro-F1 score of 70.52%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 11.48 points. The team further enhanced PeerReveal's generalization through an adversarial training framework that uses a small local generator to produce challenging reviews, raising the pooled Macro-F1 score to 82.40%. These results indicate that incorporating richer review-level evidence and adversarial training on more complex generation processes improves the robustness of AI-generated review detection.

item.title: Researchers introduce Aligned Machine, a public platform creating a Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark to evaluate semantic alignment in multimodal embedding models using human comparative judgments [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Aligned Machine is an interactive platform that gathers human comparative judgments to assess how well embedding models reflect human understanding of similarity across text and images. In an initial study with 115 participants labeling 2,875 pairs, the platform evaluated 12 popular embedding models and found only partial alignment with human judgments, with text-only models generally outperforming multimodal ones. The platform uses a forced-choice task where participants select the more similar pair between two item pairs, enabling scalable, high-confidence data collection accessible to non-experts. Results showed multimodal model alignment varies by task type, being strongest for image-image comparisons and weakest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to grow with ongoing participation, supporting longitudinal studies, bias detection, and tracking concept drift in embedding models over time.

item.title: Source-code audit and reanalysis of SkillsBench finds average skill lift of 18.7 percentage points with no statistically significant task-level reductions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers conducted a source-code-level audit and noise-aware reanalysis of SkillsBench, a benchmark measuring agent skill improvements, analyzing 7,554 public trials across 1,421 configuration-task pairs. They identified grader dependence issues, placeholder skill directories, and additional built-in skills affecting results, with an overall average skill lift of 18.7 percentage points but no statistically significant reductions in task performance after correcting for multiple tests. The audit revealed that observed negative differences in some tasks were likely due to run-sampling noise, as most cells lacked sufficient runs to detect decreases reliably. A gating strategy based on skill-free scores showed apparent improvements in logs but did not yield statistically significant gains on held-out data. The researchers have published their audit ledger and analysis scripts for transparency and further study.

item.title: Researchers analyze six reasoning language models in auction bidding, identifying model and operator errors that reduce bid surplus by up to 17% on eBay and simulated markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated six open reasoning language models with 4 billion to 14 billion parameters on auction bidding tasks using win curves from eBay and a simulated advertising market called AuctionNet. They compared model-generated bids against an exact calculator and found that models often overlooked the best bid option despite ranking it highest internally, with errors biased toward higher bids rather than position in the list. These mistakes cost bidders 7-17% of the surplus achievable by the calculator under pay-your-bid pricing. The study also identified losses due to operator choices, such as token limits truncating reasoning traces and premature answer requests before reasoning completion. Allowing models to finish reasoning improved performance significantly, with the weakest model's lead recovery doubling on both eBay and AuctionNet. An audit mechanism that flagged and corrected bids inconsistent with the model's own reasoning further increased the share of the calculator's lead recovered, demonstrating the importance of both model design and operational settings in auction bidding performance.

item.title: Researchers propose SOLO watermarking method for large language models to improve detection under repeated sampling by anchoring contexts on content via min-hash [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce SOLO, a watermarking technique for large language models that maintains a request-scoped context history anchored on content selected by min-hash to reduce response coupling and improve watermark detection. SOLO aims to preserve self-consistency and uncertainty estimation while enabling each response to be independently detectable with a single key. Evaluations on five language models across three benchmarks show SOLO detects more watermarked responses at a 1% false positive rate than existing methods, even after random token edits, with code publicly available.

item.title: MedSkill-E2 framework evaluates and improves autonomous skill use in medical AI agents, addressing skill Enable But Underuse with a new benchmark and evolution method [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce MedSkill-E2, a framework designed to evaluate and evolve skills used by large language model agents in medical tasks, focusing on the problem of skill Enable But Underuse (EBU) where agents fail to apply specified rules effectively during autonomous execution. They develop EBU-Bench, a benchmark covering 12 medical task groups, revealing a significant gap in skill-use accuracy between autonomous and guided use, averaging 43.94 percentage points across models and harnesses. To address this, the team proposes EBU-Evolve, a method that refines skill instructions using feedback from both autonomous and guided executions, resulting in improvements of 33.33 to 55.17 percentage points in autonomous skill-use accuracy. These improvements persist across different models and harnesses, demonstrating that autonomous skill-use accuracy varies with execution context and that EBU can continue even after skills are accessed. The approach also enhances performance on unseen tasks within the same skill set, indicating potential for broader application in medical AI agents.

item.title: Researchers present vSFT framework for verbally supervised fine-tuning of language model agents at test time, improving success rates on ALFWorld and WebShop tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Researchers introduce verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT), a framework that enables large language model agents to receive dense natural language feedback and update their weights during test time. The system uses a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, where verbal supervision from failed trajectories is converted into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. The vSFT approach outperforms in-context learning and common reinforcement learning methods, with the Qwen3-4B model achieving higher success rates than GRPO and Reflexion by significant margins on ALFWorld and WebShop benchmarks. The researchers suggest that learning how to adapt models dynamically at test time offers a promising direction for developing more capable self-improving agents.

item.title: INSPIRE proposes two-stage reasoning framework for forecasting emerging entities in temporal knowledge graphs, improving Emerging MRR by up to 88.83% on ICEWS and GDELT benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: INSPIRE introduces a two-stage forecasting approach to address challenges in temporal knowledge graphs where emerging entities have sparse and bursty interaction histories. The first stage learns a shared-pattern predictor with catalog-wide event memory, while the second stage optimizes an individual-evidence adapter combining semantic priors and long-range event statistics. The framework applies coordinated masking and debiasing techniques to balance support and role supervision, improving ranking of unseen answers. Evaluations on four benchmarks show INSPIRE significantly outperforms existing methods, with the individual-evidence adapter further boosting performance metrics. The code for INSPIRE is publicly available for research use.

item.title: Study measures duration perception limits in 21 multimodal large language models using melody recognition against human baseline [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researchers evaluated how 21 multimodal large language models perceive duration by testing their ability to recognize melodies slowed down at varying speeds, comparing results to human performance. Most models failed to recognize melodies without labeled in-context examples, while seven models performed reliably with such examples, generally matching median human recognition ranges. The study found that model recognition depends heavily on prompt design, with recognition peaks shifting based on example speed, prediction biases induced by melody titles, and accuracy declines at long note durations despite scientific pitch notation examples. Unlike humans, whose recognition windows are intrinsic, current models' temporal perception is largely shaped by the prompts provided.

item.title: Researchers find semantic density metrics do not predict task performance decline in LLM agent memory stores across multiple benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A study analyzed 805 snapshots from 13 memory methods used by large language model (LLM) agents across diverse environments to determine if semantic density or related statistics could warn of impending task accuracy decline. The researchers found that mean pairwise cosine similarity and other geometry, retrieval, and graph statistics did not reliably predict early performance drops, with some local crowding measures only occasionally preceding decline but not outperforming simple stored-item counts. Classifiers trained on this data and tested on extended PropWorld tasks frequently produced false alarms or missed actual declines, indicating that global semantic density is not a dependable indicator of memory collapse. The study also observed that size-limited memory stores remained stable over long task horizons, while failures occurred primarily when unbounded whole-store prompting exceeded the model's input capacity, which was directly predicted by token growth.

item.title: Verified experience improves materials prediction with large language models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33195v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Materials discovery is an iterative loop: experiments and calculations verify predictions, and each outcome can inform the next. Yet most predictors are specialized single-task models fixed after training. Large language models have recently emerged as predictors across heterogeneous tasks but generally underperform specialized models, and retrieval-augmented variants discard their own outcomes. Benchmarks also score queries in isolation, leaving improvement from outcomes untested. Here we construct MatMemBench, a sequential benchmark of 22 materials tasks that reveals outcomes only after prediction and tests online adaptation, memory retention and cross-task transfer. We present MatRecall, a framework that lets large language models store verified predictions, with evidence, outcome and error, as episodes and recall them without retraining. MatRecall improved median performance by 62% over a memory-free model, exceeded specialized models on 11 tasks, remained useful after feedback stopped and transferred between related tasks. Verified experience could become a reusable resource for self-improving discovery loops.

item.title: Extraneous Cognitive Load in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33197v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) shows that human problem-solving is affected by both intrinsic load, arising from task difficulty, and extraneous load, arising from how task information is presented. Large language models (LLMs) show analogous effects: presentation alone can affect model performance, but these effects have not yet been systematically isolated from task difficulty. To address this gap, we introduce CogLoadBench, a controlled benchmark that varies five CLT-inspired presentation factors across three reasoning task families. Across models, we find that higher extraneous load conditions often reduce accuracy by either adding competition or complicating the reasoning path. To support diagnosis and mitigation of load-related effects, we propose the Extraneous Load Score (ELS), a prompt-time metric computed from activations that estimates a model's extraneous load, and show that it generalizes across reasoning task types and load levels. We further show that shifting model representations toward lower-load directions at inference time can improve average model performance without changing prompt content.

item.title: CypherMAS: Benchmarking Routing Reliability in LLM-Based Multi-Agent Systems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33242v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) distribute reasoning across specialized agents that must exchange messages and invoke tools reliably. Existing evaluations typically couple communication with open domain tasks, making it difficult to determine whether a failure arises from reasoning, malformed tool use, lost messages, or forgotten requests. Prior benchmarks do not isolate communication execution or measure routing redundancy against a known optimal path. We introduce CypherMAS, a synthetic benchmark that isolates communication and routing in fixed multi-agent graphs. Agents in chain, star, bipartite, or ring graphs route cyphered messages to remote peers holding the matching decoders; since the optimal route is known, redundant LLM calls can be measured and routing failures may be easily tracked. Across eleven open-weight models from 4B to 753B, small models fail at routing and tool use, dense models above 27B degrade with diameter, and successful runs exceed minimum LLM calls. These findings identify communication reliability as a distinct scaling bottleneck for multi-agent systems and provide a controlled diagnostic for complex multi-agent systems. The source code is freely available: https://github.com/Andoree/CypherMAS.

item.title: When the Knowledge Runs Out: A Part-Level Pilot Evaluation of How Language Models Handle Partially Covered Questions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assistants that answer from supplied reference material often receive material that covers some parts of a user's question and not others. Existing evaluations of insufficient context mostly score one answer per question, and often treat partially sufficient context as simply insufficient. We describe a small, open evaluation that scores each part of a three-part question separately, with a verdict for parts that are answered correctly from the material but carry an added unsupported claim. On 30 cases (five scenarios, six coverage patterns, five samples each) we test claude-haiku-4-5 and llama3.1:8b. Without an explicit instruction to stay within the material, both models fill most gaps from their own knowledge (unsupported-claim rates of 0.71 and 0.90). One added sentence instructing them to answer only from the material brings these rates to 0.00 and 0.06, consistent with prior work. What remains is less visible: answers that strengthen the material, for example turning "many job sites prohibit bots" into a flat "no". We also report on the judge. Three rounds of blind hand labelling show that this added-claim verdict is the hardest to apply, for the judge and the author alike; RAGAS faithfulness is unsuitable for this task because it penalises correct withholding; and a difference between the two models that is clear under one judge disappears when the judge model is replaced. The dataset, code, hand labels and per-run figures are public.

item.title: HumblePRM: Improving VLM Abstention in Ambiguous Situations through Process Reward Modeling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33452v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable deployment of Vision Language Models (VLMs) requires that a model's expressed confidence remain grounded in what it can actually see, and that it recognize when the visual evidence is too ambiguous to commit to a confident response. Standard post-training uses outcome reward models (ORMs) that supervise only the final decision, rewarding a confident answer regardless of whether the image supports one, while existing methods either tend to detect uncertainty post-hoc or assume an objective verdict always exists. We instead split multimodal reasoning into two stages: perception, where the model must factually describe the scene, and calibration, where it must judge whether that evidence is sufficient to commit to a conclusion. We introduce HumblePRM, a lightweight process reward model (PRM) that scores each stage independently, rewarding agreement between evidence and expressed confidence rather than outcome correctness alone. Training with HumblePRM increases abstention due to uncertainty on ambiguous inputs considerably while leaving accuracy on clear images roughly unchanged. We also find that the improvement transfers to Gemma 4 E4B, a larger, popular edge model. Our findings show that process reward supervision is a promising route to VLMs with better calibrated abstention, ensuring more reliability rather than unpredictable behavior.

item.title: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33692v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.

item.title: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33700v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence. We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification. The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.

item.title: Pitfalls of Dependency-Ready Decoding for Masked Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Masked diffusion models (MDMs) have shown strong performance on structured reasoning tasks such as Sudoku, Trip Planning, and Countdown. MDMs introduce a freedom in the order in which tokens may be unmasked, and to exercise this freedom for good accuracy, early decoding strategies relied on signals of confidence or the downstream impact of decoding a token. However, simple examples seem to illustrate that resolving a token's dependencies before unmasking it should be important. Therefore, we examine whether this principle, which we call dependency-ready decoding, would contribute to better accuracy, from a practical and a theoretical perspective. We examine a recent decoder that implements dependency-readiness through attention, and generally find that when it performs better than confidence-based or future utility baselines, its decoding order collapses to left-to-right decoding. For theoretical analysis, we establish a definition of dependency without resorting to attention, measured by an information-theoretic score of how much revealing a single masked token (or a set) would shift the model's prediction for another. We prove that when the margin is large relative to this score, no such revelation can change the top prediction, so in this regime Maximum-Margin decoding already commits dependency-ready tokens. These findings leave only a narrow scope for future dependency-ready decoders: their potential benefit is limited to positions with margins smaller than the information-theoretic sensitivity, and reliance on attention should be questioned.

item.title: When Rerankers Work Together: Better and Faster Reranking without Joint Training [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33844v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standalone reranker quality does not determine its value in a multistage RAG pipeline. We systematically study heterogeneous rerankers composed without joint training, spanning lexical, single-vector, late-interaction, and joint query-context scoring. Two lightweight semantic coarse scorers, Cache-Pointwise and Cache-Shapley, learn from passage relevance labels and share cacheable representations and linear-time singleton inference. Under matched candidates and budgets, we compare cascades with stage-removal references to measure evidence retention, repair and breakage, reader accuracy, and online pruning cost. On NoLiMa 32K with Gemma, inserting these scorers before CrossEncoder or Provence improves answer accuracy by 4.02-9.43 percentage points while accelerating online pruning by 1.57-1.88x relative to the corresponding reranker alone. Cache-Pointwise composed with ColBERTv2 through reciprocal rank fusion improves accuracy by 4.60 points at 1.36x speedup over direct ColBERTv2. The stage-removal comparisons reveal an asymmetry: a cascade can outperform its final reranker alone while underperforming its coarse selector alone. Two readers, a second multi-hop dataset, and three-stage extensions show that the gains depend on the reader, reranker pairing, and stage configuration. These findings demonstrate a practical route to better and faster reranking without joint training and motivate studying stage order, candidate budgets, and rank fusion as determinants of composition quality.

item.title: DiCALM: Converting Autoregressive Convolution-Attention Language Models into Discrete Diffusion Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33919v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing methods for adapting autoregressive (AR) language models to diffusion generation focus mainly on full-attention architectures. More efficient hybrid architectures remain underexplored. We introduce DiCALM, a recipe for converting the hybrid convolution-attention models of the LFM2 family (LFM2 and LFM2.5) from AR to masked-diffusion generation. DiCALM progressively extends LFM2's causal gated convolution so that it captures local context in both directions. It combines this extension with a masking warm-up and joint AR--diffusion training. In controlled experiments, DiCALM performs comparably to the corresponding fine-tuned LFM2.5-based AR models and delivers consistent speedups over them at both the 350M and 1.2B scales: over 1.4x on average and up to 1.79x.

item.title: Fine-Tuning Without Gradients? Closed-Form, LLM-Written Classifiers on a Frozen Encoder [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.33972v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Can a classifier computed in closed form on a frozen encoder match gradient fine-tuning? We present closed-form weight-space programming (WSP): a large language model (LLM), used as a design assistant, writes programs that read a frozen masked language model through cloze-style prompt templates at several layers, fit closed-form heads (shrinkage discriminant analysis, kernel ridge regression and the encoder's label-word prior) on labelled data, and select among a pool of candidate heads by cross-fitting. No gradient is computed and no encoder weight changes. We instantiate the framework on RoBERTa-large. On 11 development datasets with 512 to 8,192 training labels, WSP is ahead of full fine-tuning (FT) and LoRA at every label budget (by 0.3 to 0.6 points on average; the registered non-inferiority tests pass) and within 0.5 points of prompt-based fine-tuning (PFT); these datasets also shaped the recipe. With fewer labels its lead over FT and LoRA grows: 1.2 to 3.5 points with 64 and 128 labels, and 3.8 to 5.3 points in the few-shot setting of 16 labels per class, where WSP is again within half a point of PFT on the development datasets. On six held-out datasets, WSP stays ahead of LoRA and within half a point of FT on average, although with six datasets no registered test passes, and PFT is ahead, by 1.30 points with 8,192 labels. WSP never collapses and is deterministic, but it needs one encoder pass per template (17 here). We report all eight recipe versions, every decision that saw test results, and 27 ideas that did not help.

item.title: Residual Cross-Model Narrative Convergence under Shared Prompts: Auditing Prompt Controls and Narrative Measurement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34015v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Stories created by LLMs based on the same prompts can be narratively similar to one another. This similarity may reflect constraints imposed by the prompts as well as the models' writing tendencies. The current research analyzes 51,240 stories created by five models in the StoryScope corpus based on 10,248 common prompts. It uses 213 narrative features in seven dimensions to compare cross-model distances between stories generated from the same prompts with distances between stories generated from different but semantically matched prompts. To assess the relationship between narrative features and prompt content, a semantic relevance mask was evaluated against 420 author-annotated prompt-feature judgments (F1 = .813; near-threshold accuracy = .621). The equally weighted mean Residual Convergence Index (RCI) was .409 without masking and .406 with masking. These findings indicate measurable cross-model narrative convergence relative to a semantically matched-prompt baseline, with little change following semantic relevance masking.

item.title: Evaluating Ukrainian Grammatical Competence in Language Models: Probability Versus Prompting [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34016v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Organisations deploying large language models in Ukrainian-language information systems need to know whether a model produces normative Ukrainian. This paper establishes a protocol for measuring that reliably and applies it to 19 models. The instrument is a released set of 1,444 Ukrainian minimal pairs covering the vocative case, numeral-noun and adjective agreement, verb government and calques from russian, with subject-verb agreement as a control; a quarter of the set was checked against the answer key in two independent native-speaker ratings, which agreed at Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.963. Every pair is scored twice: by comparing the probabilities a model assigns to the two sentences, and by asking the model directly, with the sentences presented in both orders so that answer-position effects are measured instead of being absorbed into the score. Three results follow. Order consistency (the share of pairs answered identically when the sentences are exchanged) falls below 0.05 for ten of the nineteen models, and what separates the usable models is instruction tuning, not scale. The vocative case is systematically inverted: 0.153 accuracy against 0.951 on the control, with models preferring the non-normative nominative form of address. Ukrainian adaptation substantially reduces this deficit, measured against the exact checkpoints two adapted models were trained from.

item.title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34126v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.

item.title: MINE: A Training-Free Defense against Indirect Prompt Injection via Mutual Information and Embedding Variance [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Existing defenses against indirect prompt injection in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are inherently reactive: prompt-engineering methods are often overridden by the injected instructions, while supervised detectors must be retrained for each new attack style. We propose a different paradigm: defend by maximizing relevance, not by detecting attacks. Our method, MINE, is training-free and attack-agnostic, and it also serves as a query-conditioned reranker. To evaluate defenses under realistic conditions, we introduce LC-Inj-SQuAD, a long-context benchmark with an average of 4,032 words per context. We evaluate on four datasets spanning short-context QA (Inj-SQuAD, Inj-TriviaQA), long-context QA (LC-Inj-SQuAD), and agent tool-call injection (InjecAgent). Across all four, MINE achieves the best accuracy--security trade-off among training-free defenses. It is also the only defense that stays usable against a fully adaptive attacker, generalizes to agent tool-call injection, and achieves the lowest inference latency on long contexts.

item.title: Puzzling-Bench: Evaluating Language Models on 23,777 Human-Written Puzzles with Community-Verified Answers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34331v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce Puzzling-Bench, a benchmark of 23,777 puzzles with community-verified answers drawn from the Puzzling Stack Exchange archive (2014-2026): riddles, ciphers, logic grids, lateral-thinking problems, wordplay and recreational mathematics, a third of them with images. Every puzzle carries the answer accepted by its author, a short reference answer taken from it (LLM-extracted for the evaluation sets and checked on a 50-puzzle human review), the author's own hints, community tags and a creation date, so that the benchmark supports hint ablations, category analysis and a rolling post-cutoff slice (254 puzzles posted after the training cutoff of six of the nine models we evaluate, including the best one) as a contamination check. We evaluate nine frontier and open models with a two-tier scorer (normalized exact match, then an LLM judge) and validate the judge with three judges from two model families: they agree on 95-97% of verdicts (kappa 0.82-0.96), move no model by more than 1.6 points, and show no own-family preference. The best model, GPT-6.1, reaches 74.8% on a shared 255-puzzle set; a hard core of 17 puzzles defeats all nine models; model failures are strongly correlated, and the second-best model contributes a single puzzle to a greedy ensemble, yet an oracle over all nine reaches 91%. On a 100-puzzle multimodal pilot, withholding the question's image costs the two best models 24 and 35 points. We release the dataset, the scoring pipeline and all per-row provenance.

item.title: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34398v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.

item.title: EPPC-CARE: Staged Hierarchical Annotation of Communication Behaviors in Secure Patient-Provider Messages [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34539v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Objectives: Patient portal messages provide invaluable information about communication dynamics between patients and healthcare providers, but extracting it manually is labor-intensive. We developed and evaluated EPPC-CARE, an automated framework for identifying communication behaviors together with the supporting text for each classification. Materials and Methods: From 867 messages, we obtained 5,516 reference standard annotations. Each annotation is a triplet of communication-related text (span), a broader communication category (Code), and a specific subcategory (Sub-code). We evaluated EPPC-CARE's identified triplets across six open-weight large language models (LLMs) against supervised fine-tuning and communication-based models such as EPPC-OASIS. We also compared EPPC-CARE with human expert annotations on 100 messages. Results: EPPC-CARE improved performance over EPPC-OASIS across all six models. EPPC-CARE's Triplet F1 improved by 2.90 percentage points on average, with a best score of 64.4%. On the human expert evaluation subset, EPPC-CARE and the human expert showed comparable agreement with the reference standard, with differences favoring EPPC-CARE. Discussion: These findings suggest that identifying triplet components (span, code, subcode) sequentially can improve performance across model families while preserving the supporting text behind each identification. EPPC-CARE links the communication code and subcode with the source text (span), supporting human verification of automated annotations in clinical informatics. EPPC-CARE may therefore make larger-scale studies of patient-provider communication more feasible and provide a foundation for human-in-the-loop annotation workflows. Conclusion: EPPC-CARE offers a more reliable and reviewable approach for automated characterization of communication behaviors in secure patient-provider messaging.

item.title: When the Proxy Is Wrong: Mismatch-Corrected Bandits for Adaptive Data Sampling [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34707v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Data allocation methods often use a small proxy model to select training data for a larger target model. However, this proxy can rank data differently from the target, leading to suboptimal training performance. To address this problem, we model the mismatch between the proxy and target models and incorporate it into the allocation decision. To do so, the problem is cast as a multi-fidelity bandit, where each arm is a data intervention. The proxy reward is observed every round, whereas the target reward is revealed only on rare audits of the same update. These paired observations identify arm-wise mismatches without assuming a shared offset or preservation of rankings. Mismatch-corrected bandits correct the proxy with paired residuals, audit only uncertain decisions, and pace the audit budget over training. From a theoretical viewpoint, we prove a regret decomposition and lower bounds under stationarity. These bounds show that proxy-only allocation can incur linear regret and that a minimum number of paired audits is necessary. Under abrupt changes, using the audit budget early can also incur linear regret. A sliding-window policy that spreads audits over training achieves regret of order $\sqrt{\Gamma_T T\log T}$ where $\Gamma_T$ denotes the number of change points. Experimentally, we test the approach in a closed-loop proof of concept on CivilComments-WILDS, where BERT-Small guides the training of BERT-Large. Mismatch correction improves worst-group accuracy over a target-only policy with the same target-model budget. Spreading audits over training improves worst-group accuracy by 6.3 to 10.5 percentage points at the same audit count.

item.title: Collect for Coverage, Replay with Evidence: Adaptive and Efficient On-Policy Distillation for Long-Horizon Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fully online on-policy distillation (OPD) is costly for long-horizon agents because each update depends on fresh environment rollouts. Prefix replay offers an efficient alternative by sampling current-student responses from stored histories, reducing idle time for long-tail rollouts and allowing each collected trajectory to support multiple updates. However, our analysis of the complete prefix replay pipeline identifies two limitations in long-horizon settings. In trajectory collection, teacher-only trajectories miss student-induced histories, while broader history coverage can reduce teacher reliability. In trajectory reuse, fixed position-based schedules cannot identify critical decisions that may occur at any trajectory depth. We introduce CARE-OPD (Collect for coverAge, Replay with Evidence) to address both limitations. Student-seeded teacher completions and response-level confidence gating expand history coverage while filtering unreliable updates. Hindsight replay allocation then uses downstream execution evidence to select consequential turns. Across long-horizon tasks Software Engineering and Deep Research, CARE-OPD outperforms online OPD and prior prefix replay baselines. On SWE-bench Verified, it raises task success to 59.5% while reducing end-to-end training time by 45% and environment actions by 44% relative to asynchronous online OPD.

item.title: Reading Fine-Tuning Diffs Through Lenses: Model Diffing for Backdoor Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34758v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We introduce a common scoring system based on token readouts to evaluate weight, activation and output-based model diffing methods for backdoor detection in fine-tuning processes. We also improve existing weight and activation based methods by incorporating the $J$-lens and its refinement, the $J{+}{+}$-lens. We test our setup in experiments where we compare a backdoored model with the base model from which it was fine-tuned. Our results show that incorporating the $J{+}{+}$-lens improves the weight-based method in all our settings, while the $J$-lens improves its ranks within single layers. The strongest single method is $\Delta W J{+}{+}$, the weight difference decoded through the $J{+}{+}$-lens of the base model, which ranks a token naming the backdoor among its first ten tokens in 11 of our 12 settings. Moreover, we show that output and activation based methods such as ADL and Diff Mining can easily break if the backdoored model is penalised during fine-tuning for giving the backdoor's words probability on clean inputs, whereas the weight-based methods are not affected. Conversely, permuting the hidden units or training only the layers that read the residual stream hides the backdoor from the weight-based methods but not from ADL and Diff Mining. No single method resists both attacks.

item.title: One Model, Many Modes: Evolving System Prompt Ensembles for Creative Generation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34760v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Preference-aligned LLMs can exhibit mode collapse, concentrating their output distributions around a narrow set of high-reward responses. This limits creative generation, which requires quality, novelty, and diversity. Existing test-time methods often emphasize diversity, giving less attention to whether individual responses are both high-quality and novel. This distinction matters in practical use, where users may seek a single compelling, original response. We formalize creative generation as a multi-objective distributional optimization problem and introduce SEPO, a training-free framework for System Prompt Ensemble Optimization. The framework combines prompt evolution with greedy max-min selection to identify behaviorally distinct system prompts under a quality constraint, then uniformly samples one prompt per response at inference time. Across four creative generation tasks with increasing quality requirements and three open-weight models, SEPO ranks first in 8 of 12 settings on the harmonic mean of quality, diversity, and novelty, while no baseline leads in more than two. On average, it raises LLM-judged diversity from 1.92 to 3.43 and novelty from 1.00 to 3.34 over base sampling (1-5 scale), with quality decreasing from 3.72 to 3.30. We further show that expanding the optimized ensemble increases separation among prompt-conditioned response distributions. These results support system prompt ensemble optimization as a promising approach to improving LLM creativity at inference time.

item.title: When Every Rollout Fails: Splicing Learner-Conditioned Options into Long-Horizon Agent RL [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34777v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards often yields all-fail groups on long-horizon agent tasks: every sampled trajectory receives zero reward, leaving group-relative methods without a reward-based policy gradient. A common remedy supplies complete solutions from a stronger model, but full trajectories are expensive and expose the learner to long off-policy histories. We introduce SPLICE, which constructs local training targets from failed current-policy trajectories online. For each all-fail group, a proposal model selects a splice point in a current-policy trajectory and generates several bounded options from that point. We estimate each option's value using repeated current-policy continuations, convert positive estimates into a return-weighted local target, and fit the current policy on the options. We evaluate SPLICE across two policy families on two long-horizon agent tasks, Software Engineering with SWE-bench Verified and Deep Research with BrowseComp-Plus. SPLICE outperforms GRPO and full-trajectory guidance baselines in all four settings, improving over GRPO by 2.8--9.8 percentage points. On initially failed SWE tasks, it raises GRPO's graduation rate by 10.8 percentage points. Further experiments show that SPLICE improves performance while reducing costly proposal-model computation.

item.title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models increasingly replace real people in the AI development pipeline, as they are used to generate training dialogues at scale and to drive alignment and evaluation. However, out-of-the-box models produce monolingual and stylistically flat texts as synthetic user prompts, failing to replicate the real user-AI communication mechanics. We present PersonaFactory, an end-to-end pipeline that generates detailed user personas and uses them to augment existing user prompts from their point of view, producing a bank of over 740000 structured synthetic personas detailing their background and communication behaviors, and a corpus of roughly 1.24 million persona-styled synthetic conversations spanning 85 languages. We evaluate the effect of personal features on style adoption and intent preservation, using an LLM-judge and heuristic metrics to assess augmentation fidelity together with the downstream impact on assistant persona control through training data. Results show that our structured, attribute-based style representation enables per-axis control and better intent preservation at comparable style fidelity than free-text persona descriptions used in existing methods. A human expert evaluation found the augmented conversations plausible, with favorable ratings for intent preservation, style naturalness, and multilingual authenticity. Finally, PersonaFactory conversations achieve comparable performance to original training data on capability benchmarks, are preferred on real user prompts at equal reply length, and adapt their reply style more closely to users without explicit steering.

item.title: Repairing the Trustworthiness of Distilled Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation enables the deployment of large language models through smaller student models, but the compression process can introduce regressions in trustworthiness even when downstream performance is preserved. Repairing such failures is challenging because the original distillation corpus is often unavailable, while direct preference optimization may alter capabilities inherited from the teacher. We propose a targeted repair framework based on the proximal Bregman response function (PBRF) that addresses both limitations. We estimate the curvature required for PBRF using a surrogate proxy dataset, removing dependence on the original transfer corpus, and extend the framework to preference-based supervision through an odds-ratio objective. This enables the use of preferred and dispreferred response pairs while constraining changes to the distilled model. Our results show that the proposed approach improves targeted trustworthiness behaviors for both pre-training and post-training models while largely preserving downstream performance, providing a practical alternative to re-distillation or unconstrained preference optimization. Our experiment results show that across different distilled models, the trustworthy regression can be improved by up to 8% with less than 1% decrement in perplexity.

item.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

item.title: $\mu$-Bench: Benchmarking Multi-User Task Completion in Shared Interaction Voice Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34920v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Voice agents in shared spaces must satisfy interdependent multi-user requests while upholding per-user authority, privacy, and task constraints. Existing evaluations offer limited coverage when participants react throughout a session. We introduce $\mu$-Bench, a benchmark for joint task completion in closed-loop, full-duplex multi-user voice interaction. Simulated participants act from isolated profiles of goals, knowledge, and permissions, adapting to the agent's speech and tool outcomes. Across 20 domains, 100 scenarios vary group size, acoustics, and follow-up demands to form 800 cases (408 tool-augmented, 392 tool-free). Joint Task Success (JTS) requires all user goals, privacy boundaries, and terminal states to hold jointly, while Pure JTS further disallows unauthorized tool calls; Attribution, Threading, and Coordination (ATC) diagnostics localize failures. Across 13 voice agents, proprietary systems peak at 62.24\% tool-free and 65.44\% tool-augmented success, while open-weight models remain below 20\%. ATC diagnostics show that open-weight models lag primarily in multi-turn attribution and threading, and controlled contrasts reveal that larger groups consistently degrade joint task success across capable systems. By coupling reactive multi-user simulation with verifiable session-level outcomes, $\mu$-Bench provides a rigorous testbed for shared voice agents.

item.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2611.34928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

item.title: MathArena: Evaluating LLMs on Uncontaminated Math Competitions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2505.23281v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The rapid advancement of reasoning capabilities in large language models (LLMs) has led to notable improvements on mathematical benchmarks. However, many of the most commonly used evaluation datasets (e.g., AIME 2024) are widely available online, making it difficult to disentangle genuine reasoning from potential memorization. Furthermore, these benchmarks do not evaluate proof-writing capabilities, which are crucial for many mathematical tasks. To address this, we introduce MathArena, a new benchmark based on the following key insight: recurring math competitions provide a stream of high-quality, challenging problems that can be used for real-time evaluation of LLMs. By evaluating models as soon as new problems are released, we effectively eliminate the risk of contamination. Using this framework, we find strong signs of contamination in AIME 2024. Nonetheless, evaluations on harder competitions, such as CMIMC 2025, demonstrate impressive reasoning capabilities in top-performing models. MathArena is also the first benchmark for proof-writing capabilities. On IMO 2025, top models achieve slightly less than 40%, demonstrating both notable progress and significant room for improvement. So far, we have evaluated over $50$ models across seven competitions, totaling $162$ problems. As an evolving benchmark, MathArena will continue to track the progress of LLMs on newly released competitions, ensuring rigorous and up-to-date evaluation of mathematical reasoning.

item.title: Semantic Gravity Wells: Why Negative Constraints Backfire [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2601.08070v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Negative constraints (instructions of the form "do not use word X") represent a fundamental test of instruction-following capability in large language models. Despite their apparent simplicity, these constraints fail with striking regularity, and the conditions governing failure have remained poorly understood. This paper presents a mechanistic investigation of negative instruction failure in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. We introduce semantic pressure, a quantitative measure of the model's intrinsic probability of generating the forbidden word, and show that violation probability rises with pressure ($p = \sigma(-2.95 + 2.76 P_0)$; $n=40{,}000$ samples from 2,500 prompts; prompt-bootstrap 95% CI for slope: [2.53, 3.01]), from 5% of samples at low pressure to 44% at high pressure. Comparing prompts of equal pressure, we find that the suppression induced by negative instructions is far weaker in failures: within pressure bins, the instruction lowers target probability by 0.63 less in failures than in successes (95% CI [0.61, 0.65]), and at low pressure it raises the target's probability in failures. The logit lens and direct logit attribution locate the divergence in layers 22-27, where feed-forward networks push toward the target more strongly in failures and attention pushes against it less. Activation patching shows that these late layers carry the instruction's effect in both directions. An attention-based "priming" signature does not distinguish failures from successes once its base rate is measured (90% vs. 93%); a probability-based one does (instruction raises target probability in 27% of failures vs. 13% of successes). Naming a forbidden word can prime the model to produce it, but most failures are better described as suppression that never takes hold in the final layers.

item.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Cognitive Complexity in LLMs via Linear Probing using Bloom's Taxonomy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2602.17229v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The black-box nature of Large Language Models necessitates novel evaluation frameworks that transcend surface-level performance metrics. This study investigates the internal neural representations of the levels of complexity using Bloom's Taxonomy as a hierarchical lens. By analyzing high-dimensional activation vectors from different LLMs, we probe whether different Bloom levels, ranging from basic recall (Remember) to abstract synthesis (Create), are linearly separable within the model's residual streams. Our results demonstrate that linear classifiers achieve high accuracy across all Bloom levels, providing evidence that level information is encoded in a linearly accessible subspace of the model's representations. These findings provide evidence that the model organizes representations according to Bloom categories early in the forward pass, with representations becoming increasingly separable across layers.

item.title: Search-E1: Self-Distillation Drives Self-Evolution in Search-Augmented Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2605.22511v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Outcome based reinforcement learning provides a simple and effective recipe for training search augmented reasoning agents. Recent work seeks further improvements through stronger external teachers, auxiliary process supervision, specialized reward shaping, and increasingly elaborate training pipelines. This raises a natural question: can agents continue improving by learning from their own successful experience? We present Search-E1, a simple self evolution framework that alternates vanilla GRPO with on policy self distillation (OPSD). After each GRPO round, Search-E1 mines sibling trajectories generated by the policy itself and exposes the search skeleton of an efficient successful trajectory, that is, the sequence of queries it issued, as privileged context. A token level forward KL objective then aligns the policy under its standard inference context with its own distribution under this privileged context. In this way, the policy converts contrasts among its own rollouts into dense token level supervision without an external teacher, auxiliary reward model, or annotation beyond reference answers. On seven single hop and multi hop QA benchmarks, Search-E1 reaches an average Exact Match of 0.440 with Qwen2.5-3B and 0.482 with Qwen2.5-7B, the highest seven-benchmark averages in our comparison. These results show that alternating outcome based exploration with self distillation provides a simple and effective path to iterative improvement in search augmented reasoning

item.title: A History-Aware Visually Grounded Critic for Computer Use Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2606.11078v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Various test-time interventions for Computer Use Agents (CUAs), including critic models, have been developed to improve performance through pre-execution action evaluation in complex Graphical User Interface (GUI) environments. However, existing critics suffer from two key limitations: they (1) focus primarily on short-sighted decision loops (e.g., forgetting earlier actions) and (2) lack the visual grounding needed to detect flawed actions (e.g., clicking wrong UI elements). To address these, we introduce HiViG, a History-aware Visually Grounded test-time framework, built around a multimodal critic trained on real GUI trajectories to abstract past interactions into a compact record and to evaluate actions with visual grounding. At test time, HiViG integrates the critic into the policy decision loop to provide macro-action history, which summarizes the policy's completed achievements, and visually grounded critique, which verifies raw execution coordinates against the current screenshot to intercept errors before execution. Across web, mobile, and desktop benchmarks, HiViG consistently outperforms existing scalar and verbal critics, improving average success rates over the strongest baseline by 5.8% for Qwen3-VL-32B and 9.0% for Gemini-3-Flash, and demonstrates strong cross-platform generalization. Ablations show that macro-action history mitigates short-sighted planning and visually grounded critique reduces execution errors, with both components being critical for test-time scaling in long-horizon GUI tasks.

item.title: Information Discernment in Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2607.19355v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used with external knowledge sources like the internet. Do they weigh information appropriately -- updating more for reliable sources (source discernment) and more when claims bring priors closer to the truth (truth discernment)? We formalize this as information discernment and introduce Learn2Discern (L2D), an experimental framework and benchmark grounded in three normative axioms with interpretable metrics. To establish external validity, a pre-registered, quota-matched user study (n=299) confirms that real LLM users endorse all three axioms and report that violations reduce their trust and usage intent. Across 13 models and nearly 670K trials, we find consistent failures across both dimensions: models perform near chance on source and truth discernment, rely on source popularity twice as much as source reliability, and update roughly equally whether a claim improves or worsens their position relative to the ground truth. Models integrate external knowledge most effectively on datasets where their priors are already the most accurate. Newer and larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment, a blind spot that model complexity does not address. We identify simple inference-time interventions that improve both forms of discernment. We release our dataset and survey as a testbed for a core alignment property that scales in importance as LLMs replace traditional search.

item.title: Polyrating: A Cost-Effective and Bias-Aware Rating System for LLM Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2409.00696v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rating-based human evaluation has become an essential tool to accurately evaluate the impressive performance of large language models (LLMs). However, current rating systems suffer from several important limitations: first, they fail to account for biases that significantly influence evaluation results, second, they require large and expensive preference datasets to obtain accurate ratings, and third, they do not facilitate meaningful comparisons of model ratings across different tasks. To address these issues, we introduce Polyrating, an expressive and flexible rating system based on maximum a posteriori estimation that enables a more nuanced and thorough analysis of model performance at lower costs. Polyrating can detect and quantify biases affecting human preferences, ensuring fairer model comparisons. Further, Polyrating can reduce the cost of human evaluations by up to $59\%$ for new models and up to $77\%$ for new tasks by leveraging existing benchmark scores. Lastly, Polyrating enables direct comparisons of ratings across different tasks, providing a comprehensive understanding of an LLMs' strengths, weaknesses, and relative performance across different applications.

item.title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2409.09045v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: "Silicon samples" based on large language models (LLMs) have been argued to serve as efficient alternatives to surveys of humans, assuming that their training data includes information on human attitudes and behavior. However, LLM-generated survey data might exhibit biases, for example due to a lack of diversity in training and alignment processes, which risk reinforcing existing biases in research and policymaking. In this study, we examine to what extent LLM-based predictions of individual public opinion exhibit context-dependent biases by predicting the results of the 2024 EU elections. Before the elections have taken place, we prompt three LLMs with individual-level background information of 26,000 eligible European voters to predict each person's voting behavior. We show that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt. The findings emphasize the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction. In investigating their contextual biases, this study contributes to the understanding and mitigation of inequalities in the development of LLMs and their applications in computational social science.

item.title: The Open Proof Corpus: A Large-Scale Study of LLM-Generated Mathematical Proofs [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: arXiv:2506.21621v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In recent months, large language models (LLMs) have made significant progress in mathematical proof generation, but further advancement is hindered by the lack of a large-scale, high-quality dataset of human-evaluated proofs. While expensive to create, such a dataset is essential for driving improvements in training and enabling a rigorous analysis of proof generation capabilities. In this work, we present the Open Proof Corpus (OPC), a dataset comprising over 5,000 human-evaluated proofs produced by state-of-the-art LLMs. The OPC was specifically designed for broad applicability and downstream usage in proof generation research and is the first to include a substantial number of correct, LLM-generated solutions to problems from prestigious mathematics competitions such as the USAMO and IMO. Using the OPC, we explore critical questions in automated proof generation: (1) the performance gap between natural language and formal proof generation, (2) the discrepancy between final-answer accuracy and full-proof validity, and (3) the impact of best-of-n selection on proof quality. Finally, to showcase the utility of the OPC, we finetune an 8B-parameter model on the dataset, obtaining a model that performs on par with the best model, Gemini-2.5-Pro, on the task of evaluating proof correctness.

item.title: GDS Agent for Graph Algorithmic Reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: arXiv:2508.20637v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown remarkable multimodal information processing and reasoning ability.
